We just recently use Claude Code to port an old Coldfusion site to Java Spring and it went amazingly well. It's around 50K lines of Java, one of our engineers did it in his spare time over about a week, using the $200/mo Claude plan. We had been talking about doing it for at least the last dozen years but never found the time. It would have taken around 12-18 engineer-months to do this manually.

He had the translation use browser integration to compare the new site to the old site automatically. The result was so good that he had to change background color on the new site because he couldn't be sure that he was testing the new site; it was so close to the original he was paranoid about accidentally being on the old site and not knowing it. The whole thing was done in under 2 weeks, including coding, developer testing, tester testing, and deployment. It's been in production 4-6 weeks now and we've had no reports of problems.

Translating from one language/platform to another is something AI is very very good at, so this sounds like a good use of it, bonus points if they create a comprehensive test suite first.

Yes it will lead to new bugs, but the older code probably contains a ton of bugs already and is probably difficult to update (original writers long gone, docs out of date etc), so this is probably the best way out of that situation, as long as proper support is given afterwards so they don't end up in the same situation a year later (this is the hard bit).

The ra-ra commentary from the CEO is somewhat off-putting, but the idea is not all bad.

We have an embedded system in one of product offerings that was largely developed using a bunch of “antiquated” technologies (over the past twenty years) and over the past year the two software devs that maintained it have retired. This normally would have big problem, but the entire codebase was re-written, documented, and modernized in a matter of about 3 months (for about $20k in tokens, and a mid level developer spending 50% of their time on it over that period). So it doesn’t surprise me to think a company like Cisco has piles of situations like this.

A strategy that could work very well is to let the AI

- explore the features and behaviour of the existing code

- first write lots of E2E tests for literally everything

- human-in-the-loop to review the feature list and test cases to see if some obvious or important stuff is missing

- then let implement it and verify by tests

I used this in (way) smaller scenarios and got really good examples with minimal human interaction.

I agree with the sentiments that it important to understand the code during major refactoring projects. But what if while the code was being refactored the AI was asked in addition to keep a ledger of the changes it made and why. That ledger could be the basis of providing understanding to a code base that most likely had minimal corporate understanding in the first place. And because it is ok text format, the learning scales well instead of being consolidated to a single team of people working on the project.

I don’t believe it has to be this zero sum game where either you use AI and lose understanding or you don’t use AI and gain understanding. There’s a way to do both since, if used properly, AI could be the best teacher we’ve had.

We had developed the original app in 2020-2021 when Covid was around, and we were bored sitting at home not having much to do, and wanted to learn Angular. Our employer/company we worked for, wanted all of us to be to be Full-stack and both of us were backend developers. Hence we did our dating app as a side project as my co-founder was single.

Initially it was a $100 Claude Max license, and we were maxxing it at every stage, but once rewritten, $20 is good enough to maintain it.

I think Cisco is an interesting use case for AI, because it's code, probably:

-Works according to a defined specification

-Within the bounds of that specification, has a lot of code written to optimize speed, cost, latency, etc - all measureable goals

-Written in c, with all it's weakness

-Given limitless engineering work, some could be ported to better hardware

-the new system could be automatically compared to the old system for functional correctness

All those factors fit well with agent based development.

Btw, many of them are true in general to embedded systems.
